newsitem.title: UK: One injured in fresh Northern Ireland violence.
newsitem.headline: One injured in fresh Northern Ireland violence.

text.p: Fresh violence hit Northern Ireland overnight after earlier peaceful annual parades by thousands of Protestant Orangemen loyal to Britain who agreed to avoid flashpoint Catholic areas, police said on Sunday.
In Belfast and Portadown stoning attacks were launched on Orangemen returning from parades, Britain's Press Association news agency quoted a police spokesman as saying.
One Orangeman was injured in the Portadown attack, the spokesman said. Petrol bombers attacked an Orange Order hall at Warrenpoint, damaging a car.

The leader of the pro-British Ulster Unionist Party, Northern Ireland's biggest political group, accused Irish nationalists of responding to the Orange Order's gesture of cancelling parades through Catholic areas with gunfire.
"People were asking, will there be a response from nationalists," David Trimble said at an Orange parade outside Belfast on Saturday. "Yes, there was a response, the response was gunfire."
He added: "We hope it is becoming clearer and clearer what the true nature of Sinn Fein/IRA is. The violence that came last night was not a surprise."
He was referring to Irish Republican Army guerrillas and their political allies, the Sinn Fein party, who want an end to British rule in Northern Ireland.
Two teenagers and five members of a joint police and British army patrol were injured in attacks by republican gunmen in Belfast late on Friday night.
The IRA admitted shooting the soldiers and police officers and also said it was responsible for a bomb attack on security forces.
Spokesmen for groups close to pro-British gunmen said they feared the wounding of the two teenagers, aged 14 and 18, would provoke retaliation in an atmosphere already charged with tension.
Sinn Fein president Gerry Adams called for an end to all sectarian attacks. "I appeal for calm," he said in a statement. "There should be no triumphalism, no sectarian abuse of our neighbours."
Dressed in ceremonial sashes and black bowler hats as they marched behind bands blasting out pipe and drum music, the 80,000-strong Orange Order staged parades across Northern Ireland.
Saturday's festivities commemorated a 1690 Protestant victory over Catholic forces at the Battle of the Boyne which ensured that a Protestant ascended to the British throne.
They avoided four volatile zones where parades were called off after Northern Ireland's minority Catholics threatened mass demonstrations against what they regarded as sectarian intimidation.
The decision to cancel the contentious marches in Belfast, Armagh, Newry and Londonderry exposed rifts within the fiercely pro-British Orange Order.
Hardliners accused the leadership of selling out and there were scuffles among Orangemen when they gathered for a march at the town of Limavady, the venue chosen instead of Londonderry.

An Orange leader, Grand Master Robert Saulters, called for unity, saying: "At such a time like this we ask for the wholehearted support and undivided loyalty of our brethren and all those who place confidence in us.
"Remember, 'united we stand, divided we fall'."
U.S. President Bill Clinton praised the Orange Order for rerouting its parades and condemned as "inexcusable" the attacks on security forces and the two youths.

"I welcome the decision of the Orange Order and its local lodges to voluntarily call off and reroute the contentious parades scheduled for this weekend," Clinton said in a statement as he ended an eight-day trip to Europe.

"I hope that the people of both communities redouble their efforts to reach accommodation on other contentious parades in a spirit of goodwill and generosity and reject the inexcusable violence that we saw in Northern Ireland today."
Clinton has shown particular interest in efforts to secure peace in Northern Ireland, and in 1995 became the first U.S. president to visit the troubled province.
